docs.title: 4-Stack XYZT, Skip-Counting [REP], LastX Verification & Integer Division
docs.text:
RPN PEDAGOGY // ELEMENTARY FOUNDATIONS (GRADES K–6) ● DEFAULT 4-STACK XYZT • CLASSROOM PROVEN 📖 Master Guide ⚡ RPN Power Guide 📝 120 Station Worksheets 🎯 Standards Matrix 🧑‍🏫 Teacher Guide 🏆 UIL Competition

Traditional elementary calculators force children into an algebraic syntax that creates unnecessary cognitive barriers: students struggle with hidden memory registers (M+), syntax errors caused by nested parentheses, and decimal answers when they are learning division with remainders.

In the latest system revisions, the StackCalc SC-6 Elementary Calculator standardizes on a default 4-stack XYZT live operational display for general arithmetic, while providing an automatic 2-stack mode (X, Y) for paired concrete manipulatives (such as rekenrek counting racks and two-dice probability tables). Users and teachers can also toggle back to 2-stack mode whenever desired. This guide explains the mathematical and pedagogical rationale behind this architecture, and provides classroom-ready teaching modules for core RPN elementary capabilities:

  1. The 4-Stack XYZT Visual Model & 2-Stack Manipulative Modes: Visual permanence for multi-step arithmetic, with focused 2-line views for paired entry.
  2. Integer Division with Remainders ([÷R]): Simultaneous quotient (\(X\)) and remainder (\(Y\)) display.
  3. Instant Inverse Verification ([LASTX]): Concrete student self-checking without teacher intervention.
  4. Rhythmic Skip-Counting ([REP]): Auditory and tactile reinforcement of multiplication facts.

docs.title: 1. Why 4-Stack XYZT is the Default in Elementary Math
docs.text:
In early prototype testing, a 2-line display was considered for simplicity. However, empirical classroom trials across Grades 3–6 revealed that a 4-level XYZT stack is dramatically more intuitive for young learners for three fundamental reasons:

+-------------------------------------------------------+
|  HIGH-CONTRAST MONOCHROME LCD (TERMINUS PIXEL FONT)   |
+-------------------------------------------------------+
|  T:        12.0000   <-- Top / Overflow Memory Level  |
|  Z:        35.0000   <-- Suspended Subtotal Level     |
|  Y:         3.0000   <-- Active Remainder / Operand 1 |
|  X:         5.0000   <-- Active Input / Quotient      |
+-------------------------------------------------------+

docs.title: 1.1 Cognitive Load & Visual Permanence
docs.text:
On a standard calculator, intermediate calculations vanish. In a problem like: $\((4 \times 8) + (15 \div 3)\)$ a student evaluating \(4 \times 8 = 32\) must either write \(32\) down on scratch paper, memorize it in short-term memory, or master obscure memory keys (STO, RCL, M+).

On the SC-6, evaluating 4 [ENTER] 8 [×] leaves 32 sitting visibly in the stack. When the student types 15 [ENTER] 3 [÷], 32 gently slides up to Register \(Y\), while 5 appears in Register \(X\). Both numbers remain simultaneously visible on the screen. Pressing [+] (full sequence: 4 [ENTER] 8 [×] 15 [ENTER] 3 [÷] [+]) combines them to yield 37. Zero writing, zero memory keys, zero working memory fatigue.

docs.title: 1.2 Zero Parentheses Syntax Errors
docs.text:
Elementary students have not mastered algebraic formal syntax. On standard in-fix calculators, entering: $\(2 + 3 \times 4\)$ yields either 20 (on cheap non-precedence calculators) or 14 (on algebraic hierarchy machines), creating profound confusion about what the machine is actually doing. In RPN, there is strictly no ambiguity and no parentheses keys: * If you mean add first: 2 [ENTER] 3 [+] 4 [×] = 20 * If you mean multiply first: 3 [ENTER] 4 [×] 2 [+] = 14

The student controls the order of operations explicitly, mirroring the natural mental decomposition taught in Singapore Math and Bridges.

docs.title: 1.3 Uniformity Across the K–12 Continuum
docs.text: By standardizing on a 4-stack XYZT display from Grade 1, students develop an intuitive spatial mental model of the stack that carries forward seamlessly to the flagship SC-32 Scientific Calculator in middle school, high school AP Physics, and collegiate engineering. There is zero unlearning.

docs.title: 1.4 Two-Stack Mode for Special Manipulative Entries & Stack Depth Rubric
docs.text: While the 4-stack XYZT architecture is the default for general multi-step arithmetic, early elementary concrete manipulatives are frequently binary: * Counting Racks & Dual Ten-Frames (Rekenreks): A standard counting rack has two rows of beads (top wire and bottom wire). When using counting rack and ten-frame shelf entry modes ([▦] or [g] [COUNT]), the SC-6 automatically focuses on a Two-Stack Display (\(Y, X\)). The top row maps directly to Register \(Y\) and the bottom row maps to Register \(X\). This creates an exact 1:1 spatial correspondence between the physical beads and the screen without the distraction of upper registers (\(Z, T\)). * Two-Dice Probability & Domino Pairs: Pressing [🎲] generates random rolls directly in a focused 2-stack view, where Die 1 registers in \(Y\) and Die 2 registers in \(X\). Combining them ([+]), finding their difference ([-]), or computing products ([×]) is immediate and uncluttered. * Returning to Standard 4-Stack Number Mode: Pressing [NUM] (Whole Number Mode key at Row 3 Col 4) or [FDISP] immediately exits manipulative mode and restores the default 4-stack XYZT operational display. * Manual Stack Depth Switching ([FLAGS] Key Rubric): Kindergarten and early Grade 1 teachers who want to keep cognitive load minimal across all arithmetic operations can manually switch the SC-6 into 2-stack mode at any time using the hardware configuration rubric: 1. Press [g] [FLAGS] to open the system configuration matrix. 2. Press digit [5] (5:DEP) to cycle stack depth between 4-LV (4-level XYZT) and 2-LV (2-level \(Y, X\)). 3. Press [C] (or [g] [FLAGS]) to dismiss the flags matrix and resume calculations with the chosen stack depth. (In the desktop and companion apps, clicking the LCD stack depth badge or opening the Flags menu provides the same direct toggle.)

docs.title: 2. Curricular Module 1: Integer Division with Remainders ([÷R])
docs.text: // STANDARDS ALIGNMENT CCSS-M: 4.OA.A.3, 4.NBT.B.6, 5.NBT.B.6 • TEKS: 4.4E, 4.4F, 5.3C • Singapore: Primary 3A Ch 3, Primary 4A Ch 2

docs.title: The Elementary Division Dilemma
docs.text:
In Grades 3 through 5, division is introduced as fair sharing with leftovers (quotient and remainder): $\(23 \div 4 = 5 \text{ R } 3\)$ When an elementary student enters \(23 \div 4\) on a standard smartphone or cheap school calculator, the screen displays: $\(5.75\)$ For a 9-year-old who has not yet learned decimal place value or fraction-to-decimal conversion, \(5.75\) is actively counter-productive. It fails to answer: * "How many full boxes of 4 can we pack?" (5 boxes) * "How many items are left over?" (3 items, not 0.75 items!)

Because of this, teachers routinely ban calculators during division units.

docs.title: The SC-6 Solution: The [÷R] Integer Division Key
docs.text:
The SC-6 provides a dedicated Integer Division with Remainder operator located at [g] [÷R] (legend ÷R):

        DIVIDEND                 DIVISOR                     OPERATION
   [2] [3] [ENTER]                 [4]                   [g] [÷R]  (÷R)
          |                         |                          |
          v                         v                          v
+-----------------+       +-----------------+        +-----------------+
| T:         0    |       | T:         0    |        | T:         0    |
| Z:         0    |       | Z:         0    |        | Z:         0    |
| Y:        23    |       | Y:        23    |        | Y:         3  <-- REMAINDER
| X:        23    |       | X:         4    |        | X:         5  <-- QUOTIENT
+-----------------+       +-----------------+        +-----------------+

docs.title: Keystroke Protocol & Display State
docs.text:
1. Enter Dividend: Type 23, press [ENTER].
  2. Enter Divisor: Type 4.
  3. Execute Integer Division: Press [g] [÷R] (full sequence: 23 [ENTER] 4 [g] [÷R]).
  4. Immediate Result:
  5. Register X displays the Quotient (5).
  6. Register Y displays the Remainder (3).
  7. Both values are visible at the same moment on the 4-line display!

docs.title: Swapping Quotient and Remainder ([x⇄y])
docs.text: If a follow-up calculation requires the remainder, the student does not need to retype it. Simply press [x⇄y] (the primary swap key): * X becomes 3 (Remainder ready for computation) * Y becomes 5 (Quotient preserved in stack)

docs.title: Classroom Investigation: Spool Slicing & Filament Leftovers
docs.text:
Scenario: A 5th-grade maker lab has a 1,000-gram spool of Sunlu Midnight Navy PLA filament. Each 3D-printed calculator housing requires exactly 82 grams. 1. How many complete calculator housings can the class 3D print? 2. How many grams of filament remain on the spool for calibration test chips?

  • Verified Keystroke Sequence: 1000 [ENTER] 82 [g] [÷R]
  • Verified Quotient (\(X\)): 12 complete calculator chassis printed!
  • Verified Remainder (\(Y\)): 16 grams of scrap / test filament remaining (T: 0 | Z: 0 | Y: 16 | X: 12).

docs.title: 3. Curricular Module 2: Instant Inverse Verification with [LASTX]
docs.text: // STANDARDS FOR MATHEMATICAL PRACTICE CCSS.MATH.PRACTICE.MP1: Make sense of problems and persevere in solving them. CCSS.MATH.PRACTICE.MP3: Construct viable arguments and critique the reasoning of others. CCSS.MATH.PRACTICE.MP6: Attend to precision.

docs.title: The Misconception: "I Got an Answer, So I'm Done"
docs.text:
A persistent struggle in elementary math is teaching students to check their work using inverse operations: $\(\text{If } A + B = C \implies C - B = A\)$ $\(\text{If } A \times B = C \implies C \div B = A\)$

On standard calculators, as soon as the user presses =, the input operands vanish into the ether. Checking the answer requires re-entering the entire problem from scratch, which students find tedious and resist doing.

docs.title: The SC-6 Solution: The [LASTX] Key
docs.text:
The SC-6 maintains a hardware memory register called LASTX. Whenever an arithmetic operation (+, -, ×, ÷, ÷R, MOD) is executed, the calculator automatically copies the value that was in Register \(X\) right before the calculation into LASTX.

Pressing [f] [LASTX] pushes that saved operand back into Register \(X\), lifting the answer into Register \(Y\)!

docs.title: Recipe 1: Self-Checking Multi-Digit Addition
docs.text:
Student Task: Solve \(487 + 265\) and verify using inverse subtraction (487 [ENTER] 265 [+] [f] [LASTX] [-] → 487).

PHASE 1: SOLVE THE ADDITION
1. [4] [8] [7] [ENTER]    --> Y: 487 | X: 487
2. [2] [6] [5]            --> Y: 487 | X: 265
3. [+]                    --> X: 752  (Sum)
   [Calculator quietly stores 265 in LASTX]

PHASE 2: VERIFY WITH INVERSE SUBTRACTION (ONE KEYSTROKE!)
4. [f] [LASTX]            --> Y: 752 | X: 265  (Original addend retrieved!)
5. [-]                    --> X: 487  (Original starting number restored!)

Teacher Facilitation Prompt: "Did your screen return to 487? If yes, your addition is mathematically guaranteed to be correct. You proved it yourself without asking the teacher!"

docs.title: Recipe 2: The Complete Division Proof (\(Q \times D + R = \text{Dividend}\))
docs.text:
Student Task: Divide \(79 \div 8\) using [g] [÷R], then prove the result using [f] [LASTX] (79 [ENTER] 8 [g] [÷R] [f] [LASTX] [×] [+] → 79).

PHASE 1: INTEGER DIVISION
1. [7] [9] [ENTER] [8] [g] [÷R]
   SCREEN READOUT:
   Y: 7  (Remainder R)
   X: 9  (Quotient Q)
   [LASTX automatically holds the Divisor: 8]

PHASE 2: THE 3-KEYSTROKE PROOF
2. [f] [LASTX]            --> Z: 7 (R) | Y: 9 (Q) | X: 8 (Divisor D)
3. [×]                    --> Y: 7 (R) | X: 72 (Q × D)
4. [+]                    --> X: 79  (Original Dividend restored!)

This 3-keystroke verification sequence ([f] [LASTX] → [×] → [+]) concretizes the Division Algorithm identity: $\(\text{Dividend} = (\text{Quotient} \times \text{Divisor}) + \text{Remainder}\)$ Students actively experience how multiplication and addition undo division and subtraction.

docs.title: Recipe 3: Recovering from a Keystroke Slip
docs.text:
Elementary students frequently press the wrong operator by mistake (e.g., hitting [-] instead of [+]). On traditional calculators, they must press CLEAR and start over. On the SC-6 (150 [ENTER] 25 [-] [f] [LASTX] [+] [f] [LASTX] [+] → 175):

  • Problem: Student wants \(150 + 25\).
  • Mistake: They enter 150 [ENTER] 25 [-] and get 125.
  • Recovery:
  • Press [f] [LASTX] → 25 returns to \(X\), 125 lifts to \(Y\).
  • Press [+] → 150 (Starting base restored!).
  • Press [f] [LASTX] → 25 returns to \(X\), 150 lifts to \(Y\).
  • Press [+] → 175 (Correct sum reached without re-typing 150 or 25!).

docs.title: 4. Curricular Module 3: Rhythmic Skip-Counting with [REP]
docs.text: // STANDARDS ALIGNMENT CCSS-M: 2.OA.C.4, 3.OA.A.1, 3.OA.A.7 • Bridges: Grade 2 Unit 1, Grade 3 Unit 2 • Singapore: Primary 2A Ch 4, Primary 3A Ch 3

docs.title: Why Kinesthetic Rhythm Matters
docs.text:
Multiplication is fundamentally equal groups of items. Before children can memorize \(7 \times 6 = 42\), they must feel and hear the cadence of the sequence: $\(7, 14, 21, 28, 35, 42\)$

The SC-6 features a dedicated Replication Key [REP] located at [g] [REP]. Pressing [g] [REP] populates every level of the 4-level stack with the active number: $\(T = K, \quad Z = K, \quad Y = K, \quad X = K\)$

Because an RPN 4-stack duplicates the \(T\) register when the stack drops during dyadic addition, pressing [+] repeatedly adds the constant indefinitely!

                     HOW [REP] CREATES AN INFINITE FACT LADDER

1. [7] [g] [REP]           2. PRESS [+]              3. PRESS [+] AGAIN
+---------------------+    +---------------------+    +---------------------+
| T:         7        |    | T:         7        |    | T:         7        |
| Z:         7        |    | Z:         7        |    | Z:         7        |
| Y:         7        |    | Y:         7        |    | Y:         7        |
| X:         7        |    | X:        14  (7×2) |    | X:        21  (7×3) |
+---------------------+    +---------------------+    +---------------------+
                                 (T duplicates on drop!)    (T duplicates on drop!)

docs.title: Classroom Activity: The Rhythm of Multiples
docs.text:
1. Teacher Prompt: "Let's build the 6-times multiplication ladder up to 60."
  2. Setup: Student types 6 [g] [REP]. All 4 stack registers are now primed with 6.
  3. Execution: The student chants aloud with each tactile snap:
  4. Press [+] → "6 times 2 is 12!" (Screen: 12)
  5. Press [+] → "6 times 3 is 18!" (Screen: 18)
  6. Press [+] → "6 times 4 is 24!" (Screen: 24)
  7. Press [+] → "6 times 5 is 30!" (Screen: 30)
  8. Press [+] → "6 times 6 is 36!" (Screen: 36)
  9. Press [+] → "6 times 7 is 42!" (Screen: 42)
  10. Press [+] → "6 times 8 is 48!" (Screen: 48)
  11. Press [+] → "6 times 9 is 54!" (Screen: 54)
  12. Press [+] → "6 times 10 is 60!" (Screen: 60)

The 400-gram snap-dome keys deliver an audible acoustic "click" and physical tactile feedback that anchors the auditory chant to muscle memory.

docs.title: Exploration A: Backwards Countdown Ladders (Subtracting Constantly)
docs.text: Task: Start at 100, skip-count backwards by 8. 1. Enter starting point: 100 [ENTER]. 2. Prime the subtrahend: 8 [g] [REP]. 3. Press [-] repeatedly: * Press [-] → 92 * Press [-] → 84 * Press [-] → 76 * Press [-] → 68 ... down to 4 (the remainder of \(100 \div 8\)!).

docs.title: Exploration B: Geometric Exponential Doubling (Powers of 2)
docs.text: Task: Discover exponential growth (doubling lily pads on a pond). 1. Prime the base: 2 [g] [REP]. 2. Press [×] repeatedly: * Press [×] → 4 (\(2^2\)) * Press [×] → 8 (\(2^3\)) * Press [×] → 16 (\(2^4\)) * Press [×] → 32 (\(2^5\)) * Press [×] → 64 (\(2^6\)) * Press [×] → 128 (\(2^7\)) ... up to 1024 (\(2^{10}\))!

docs.title: 5. Curricular Module 4: Order of Operations without Parentheses
docs.text: // STANDARDS ALIGNMENT CCSS-M: 5.OA.A.1, 6.EE.A.2 • Big Ideas Math: Grade 5 Ch 1, Grade 6 Ch 3

docs.title: Multi-Term Word Problem Example
docs.text:
Scenario: A school STEM club buys: * 3 microcontrollers at $4.50 each * 2 battery holders at $1.25 each * 4 LED packs at $0.75 each

What is the total cost of the order? $\(\text{Total} = (3 \times 4.50) + (2 \times 1.25) + (4 \times 0.75)\)$

docs.title: How Infix vs. SC-6 4-Stack Handles the Problem (3 [ENTER] 4.5 [×] 2 [ENTER] 1.25 [×] [+] 4 [ENTER] 0.75 [×] [+] → 19)
docs.text:
Step Traditional Infix Calculator SC-6 4-Stack XYZT (RPN) Stack Registers (\(T, Z, Y, X\)) 1 Press ( 3 × 4.50 ) + (Must remember parentheses!) 3 [ENTER] 4.5 [×] \(X: 13.50\) 2 Press ( 2 × 1.25 ) + (Hope parentheses don't nest wrong!) 2 [ENTER] 1.25 [×] \(Y: 13.50, \quad X: 2.50\) 3 Press ( 4 × 0.75 ) = [+] \(X: 16.00\) (Running total!) 4 Hope order-of-operations evaluated correctly 4 [ENTER] 0.75 [×] \(Y: 16.00, \quad X: 3.00\) 5 — [+] \(X: 19\) (Final total verified!)

The Pedagogical Difference: On the SC-6, students never type a parenthesis. Every sub-calculation is evaluated immediately, and the intermediate products wait patiently on the stack. The child can pause at Step 2 and see both $13.50 and $2.50 resting on the screen.

docs.title: Challenge Card 1: The Cookie Bakery Box Packing (Grades 3–4)
docs.text: Prompt: A baker bakes 58 chocolate chip cookies. Each gift box holds 6 cookies. 1. Use [g] [÷R] on your SC-6 to find how many full gift boxes she can pack. 2. How many cookies are left over for the baker to eat? 3. Press [f] [LASTX] [×] [+] to prove your answer matches 58! Expected Keystrokes: 58 [ENTER] 6 [g] [÷R] ==> X: 9 boxes, Y: 4 leftover cookies. Proof: 58 [ENTER] 6 [g] [÷R] [f] [LASTX] [×] [+] ==> 58 cookies.

docs.title: Challenge Card 2: The Multiplication Table 7s Race (Grades 2–3)
docs.text: Prompt: Load 7 into your SC-6 using [g] [REP]. 1. Press [+] four times. What multiple of 7 is on the screen? (\(7 \times 5 = 35\)) 2. Press [+] three more times. What is \(7 \times 8\)? (\(56\)) 3. Can you reach 70 without making an error? Expected Keystrokes: 7 [g] [REP] [+] [+] [+] [+] ==> 35. [+] [+] [+] ==> 56.

docs.title: Challenge Card 3: The Detective Proof Station (Grades 4–5)
docs.text: Prompt: A student calculated \(345 + 189 = 534\). 1. Enter 345 [ENTER] 189 [+] on your SC-6. 2. Use [f] [LASTX] to recall the second addend. 3. Press [-] to perform the inverse operation (345 [ENTER] 189 [+] [f] [LASTX] [-]). Did you get 345? 4. Write an explanation: Why does LASTX guarantee the answer is correct?

docs.title: Summary: Empowering Young Mathematicians
docs.text: The transition to a default 4-stack XYZT display in the SC-6 transforms the calculator from a passive answer generator into an active, transparent laboratory instrument. With [÷R], [LASTX], and [REP], young students explore the fundamental structures of arithmetic—quotients, remainders, inverses, and multiples—with tactile certainty and joy.

docs.title: The Three Most Common Student Traps & Quick Verbal Cues
Trap 1: The "Where is the Equals Key?" Reflex
docs.text:
• What Happens: The student enters 3 [ENTER] 5 [+] and then sits staring at the keypad, asking why the calculator hasn't calculated the answer yet.
  • The Cause: 10+ years of conditioning on standard in-fix keyboards where nothing happens until you press =.
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "Point to your desk: when you drop 5 marbles into a jar that already has 3 marbles, do you have to press a button to make 8 marbles appear? No—combining them IS the answer! The [+] button did the combining. Look at the screen: 8 is already sitting right there in Register X!"

docs.title: Trap 2: The "Double Enter" Accidental Stack Lift
docs.text:
• What Happens: The student wants to calculate \(4 + 7\). They type 4 [ENTER] 7 [ENTER] [+] and get 14 instead of 11.
  • The Cause: The student mistakenly treats [ENTER] like a comma after every single number. The second [ENTER] duplicated the 7 into Register Y, pushing 4 up to Register Z. When they pressed [+], the calculator evaluated \(7 + 7 = 14\).
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "Look at the 4 stack lines on your screen. [ENTER] is the elevator door: it lifts your first number up so you have room to type the second number on Line 1. You only need the elevator once between numbers! Type 4 [ENTER] 7 [+] (11)."

docs.title: Trap 3: The "Larger Denominator Means Bigger Fraction" Fallacy
docs.text:
• What Happens: When comparing \(\frac{1}{8}\) and \(\frac{1}{3}\), the student asserts that \(\frac{1}{8}\) is larger because \(8 > 3\).
  • The Cause: Over-reliance on abstract symbolic digits without spatial intuition.
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "Don't look at the paper. Pick up the \(\frac{1}{8}\) block in your left hand and the \(\frac{1}{3}\) block in your right hand. Stand them side-by-side on your desk workbench lid. Run your index finger across them. Which one is taller? The block cannot lie."

docs.title: Trap 4: The "Factor Addition vs Multiplicative Height" Trap
docs.text:
• What Happens: When working with Prime Factor Studio, a student stacks a 2 block and a 3 block and expects the height to measure \(5\) on the scale rather than \(6\).
  • The Cause: Habituation to linear addition rods (like Counting Tiles or Cuisenaire rods) rather than logarithmic factor scaling.
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "Remember: prime blocks do not add—they multiply! When you stack a 2 block on a 3 block, you are physically multiplying: \(2 \times 3 = 6\). Compare your stack to the Composite 6 height or Factor Lid socket: the stack levels perfectly flush! Press 6 [g] [FACT] on your SC-6 to see your factors verified on the LCD."

docs.title: RPN Classroom Superpowers: Teaching with the 4-Stack XYZT Engine
docs.text:
In the latest system revisions, the StackCalc SC-6 Elementary Calculator standardizes on a default 4-stack XYZT live operational display. Unlike cheap algebraic calculators that force children to grapple with parentheses or hide intermediate steps, the 4-level stack makes mathematics visible and concrete.

[!TIP] Two-Stack Mode for Number Racks & Dice (Plus Teacher Toggle): While standard number mode defaults to the 4-level XYZT stack, special entry modes automatically switch to a focused 2-Stack Mode (\(Y, X\)) for paired concrete manipulatives—such as 2-row rekenrek counting racks ([▦] or [g] [COUNT]) and two-dice probability stations ([🎲]). Pressing [NUM] immediately returns to 4-stack mode. Kindergarten and Grade 1 teachers can also manually set the calculator into 2-stack mode across all operations via the configuration rubric: press [↱] [FLAGS] → [5] (5:DEP) → [C] to reduce visual complexity for early learners.

For the complete curricular framework, see the RPN Elementary Power Guide →. Here are the four essential classroom techniques to introduce to your students:

docs.title: Superpower 1: Rhythmic Skip-Counting & Multiplication Fact Ladders ([REP])
docs.text:
• The Math Concept: Multiplication is repeated equal groups (\(7 \times 4 = 7 + 7 + 7 + 7\)).
  • How to Do It:
  • Student enters the step size: 7 [g] [REP]. All 4 stack levels (\(T, Z, Y, X\)) fill with 7.
  • Press [+] repeatedly: 14, 21, 28, 35, 42...
  • Why It Works: In HP-standard 4-level RPN, the \(T\) register is automatically duplicated during stack drops, creating an infinite constant addition ladder.
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "Listen to the click! With every press of [+], chant the fact out loud: '7 times 2 is 14, 7 times 3 is 21...' Your fingers and ears are learning the multiples together."

docs.title: Superpower 2: Integer Division with Remainders ([÷R])
docs.text:
• The Math Concept: Elementary division is fair-sharing with leftovers (\(23 \div 4 = 5 \text{ R } 3\)). Standard calculators show \(5.75\), confusing students who haven't studied decimals.
  • How to Do It:
  • Enter dividend and divisor: 23 [ENTER] 4.
  • Execute integer division: [↱] [÷R] (so the full sequence is 23 [ENTER] 4 [g] [÷R]).
  • Read the screen:
    • Line X: 5 (The Whole Quotient \(Q\))
    • Line Y: 3 (The Remainder \(R\))
    • Both numbers appear simultaneously on the 4-line display!
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "Look at your two bottom lines: Line X tells you how many full cookies each friend gets (5). Line Y tells you how many cookies are left in the jar (3). No decimals, no confusion!"

docs.title: Superpower 3: Instant Self-Checking via [LASTX] ([↰] [LASTX])
docs.text:
• The Math Concept: Mathematical practice standard MP3 & MP6—verifying calculations using inverse operations (\(A + B = C \implies C - B = A\)).
  • How to Do It:
  • Student calculates \(48 + 37\): 48 [ENTER] 37 [+] → 85.
  • Press [↰] [LASTX]: The calculator recalls 37 into Register \(X\), lifting 85 into Register \(Y\).
  • Press [-] (full sequence: 48 [ENTER] 37 [+] [f] [LASTX] [-]): The screen immediately returns to 48!
  • Division Proof (\(Q \times D + R = \text{Dividend}\)):
  • After \(79 \div 8\) (X: 9, Y: 7), press [↰] [LASTX] (retrieves Divisor 8) [×] [+] → 79 (reconstructs the starting dividend in 3 keys!).
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "Before raising your hand to ask if your answer is right, press [LASTX] and the opposite sign. If your original number comes back, you have proven your own math!"

docs.title: Superpower 4: Parenthesis-Free Multi-Step Problem Solving
docs.text:
• The Math Concept: Evaluating multi-step expressions like \((4 \times 8) + (15 \div 3)\) without parentheses errors.
  • How to Do It:
  • Calculate first chunk: 4 [ENTER] 8 [×] → 32 in \(X\).
  • Calculate second chunk: 15 [ENTER] 3 [÷] → 5 in \(X\), 32 lifts to \(Y\).
  • Combine chunks (4 [ENTER] 8 [×] 15 [ENTER] 3 [÷] [+]): [+] → 37 in \(X\).
  • The 5-Second Teacher Cue:

    "Notice how the stack holds your first answer safely on Line 2 while you solve Line 1. When both parts are ready, just press [+] to snap them together."

docs.text:
In Texas UIL and TMSCA Calculator Applications, competitors have exactly 30 minutes to complete 70 rigorous problems. \[ \text{Problem 14: } \frac{4.82 \times 10^3 - 195}{\sqrt{84.6} + 12.7^2} \]

docs.title: Contest Coaching & Sprint Pacing Strategies

docs.text: Pages 1 and 2 consist of straightforward numerical calculations. Contestants should complete all 20 problems in under 7 minutes. Because RPN eliminates parentheses, keystroke cadence should be fluid and rhythmic. Aim for \(100\%\) accuracy here, yielding \(+100\) baseline points.

docs.title: 2. The Word Problem Filter (Minutes 7:00 – 16:00)
docs.text: Pages 3 and 4 introduce stated word problems and first-tier geometry (triangles, rectangles). Contestants should read the word problem, extract the required formula, execute the RPN chain, and write down the 3-sig-fig answer immediately without writing scratch equations.

docs.title: 3. The Geometry Vector Sweep (Minutes 16:00 – 24:00)
docs.text: Page 5 contains geometric figures (frustums, circular sectors). Train competitors to solve from the inside out: compute radius subtractions first, stack the result, multiply by slant height, and terminate with [↱] [π] and [×].

docs.title: 4. The Final Push & Strategic Stopping (Minutes 24:00 – 30:00)
docs.text: Under UIL scoring rules, an unattempted question incurs zero penalty, while an incorrect guess costs \(-4\) points. In the final 2 minutes, competitors should never make blind guesses. Once they reach their peak problem, they should stop cleanly to avoid negative deductions.

docs.title: StackCalc32: A Tactile RPN Calculator
docs.text:
// HACKADAY.IO PROJECT · BUILD LOG ARCHIVE

Project Page: https://hackaday.io/project/206743-stackcalc32-a-tactile-rpn-calculator Status: Mechanical Prototype Verified · Custom RP2350 PCB in Fabrication

docs.title: 1. Project Overview
docs.text:
Reverse Polish Notation (RPN) eliminated parentheses in the golden age of scientific computing, yet modern students are still forced into nested syntax traps. StackCalc32 redesigns the RPN calculator from the ground up: starting with an ultra-constrained Apple Watch UI, extending to a shared clean-room Swift core (RPNCore), and culminating in an open-hardware pocket calculator powered by the Raspberry Pi RP2350 microcontroller.

The mechanical enclosure uses a novel tool-free 4-part sliding rail system. The custom 4-layer PCB is currently in fabrication at the board house; visible hardware photos represent unpowered 3D-printed mechanical prototypes used for ergonomic and tolerance validation.

docs.title: 2. Current Prototype & Evidence Boundaries
docs.text: We hold our documentation to a strict standard of engineering truthfulness: - Board Design Status: The 4-layer custom KiCad RP2350 PCB design is complete and currently in fabrication at the factory. There is no powered physical board on the desk yet. - Physical Photos: All hardware photos in this project show the 3D-printed tool-free mechanical prototype (chassis_award, unified_faceplate_award, tpu_membrane_award, top_cap_award). These parts are unpowered and evaluate rail sliding tolerances, membrane fit, and snap closure. - Firmware Verification: The firmware logic, display driver, and keyboard matrix scanner are tested and verified via a native WebAssembly and RP2350 software emulator subjected to 40 Hz differential grammar fuzzing. - Companion Apps: Full v1.1 versions of StackCalc are available on the Apple App Store for iPhone, iPad, and Apple Watch.

docs.title: Board Arrival Evidence Protocol & Checklist
docs.text:
// HARDWARE BRING-UP · GATED EVIDENCE PROTOCOL

Hardware Gate Constraint: A booted screen does not prove keypad reliability or battery endurance. Each physical property must be inspected and recorded as an independent test observation before making public hardware claims.

docs.title: The Seven Verification Stages
docs.text: Stage Inspection Target Verification Method Acceptance Threshold Failure Condition & Triage 1. Seating Plane PCB fit into chassis rails Slide board into chassis_award guide channels. Measure perimeter gap. Board seats flush on internal shelf; zero lateral rocking; \(\le 0.20\text{ mm}\) gap. Rail binding -> Measure caliper width of PCB routing edge. Sand or adjust CAD. 2. Display Alignment 2.5" ST7567 LCD centering Mount LCD in faceplate cowl. Inspect viewing window margins with backlit test pattern. Active display area centered within \(\pm 0.3\text{ mm}\); zero pixel cutoff by bezel cowl. Misaligned window -> Adjust faceplate aperture in unified_faceplate_award.scad. 3. Connector Clearance 0.5 mm ZIF ribbon loop Insert FFC into bottom-contact ZIF socket. Slide assembly closed. Ribbon maintains natural \(\ge 1.5\text{ mm}\) radius bend; zero pinching against chassis rib. Creased ribbon -> Immediate stop; deepen chassis relief notch. 4. Matrix / Switch Reach Key actuator contact Depress each of the 37 keys through TPU membrane. Inspect switch plunger contact. Every key achieves tactile dome click with \(\le 1.8\text{ mm}\) travel; zero key binds against aperture. Switch not engaging -> Check actuator stem height on tpu_membrane_award.scad. 5. Cap Closure & Retention Snap-retention top cap Slide top_cap_award into place. Measure retention force with pull gauge. Audible dual-snap engagement; withstands \(\ge 15\text{ N}\) pull force without popping open. Loose cap -> Increase detent engagement lip by \(+0.15\text{ mm}\). 6. Powered Boot & Current USB-C power-up & quiescent draw Connect current-limited DC bench supply (3.3V, 100mA limit). Flash UF2 test image. Boot banner appears; quiescent current \(\le 18\text{ mA}\) at 133 MHz; zero thermal runaway. Short circuit / high current -> Immediate power cut; inspect for soldering bridges. 7. First Calculation Operational stack execution Execute standard golden keystroke sequence: 2 [ENTER] 3 [+] and verify screen. Screen displays exact integer 5 in X register; stack lifts cleanly; zero debounce ghosting. Calculation error or ghost keys -> Check matrix diode orientation and software debounce timer.

docs.title: StackCalc32 Build Instructions
docs.text:
// HACKADAY.IO · BUILD INSTRUCTIONS

Current Hardware Stage: The custom RP2350 PCB is in fabrication. These build directions cover Phase 1: 3D printing and mechanical assembly of the four-part tool-free prototype (chassis_award, unified_faceplate_award, tpu_membrane_award, top_cap_award). Electrical assembly instructions will be released in Phase 2 once verified boards arrive.

docs.title: Materials & Tools
docs.text:
• 3D Printer: \(\ge 180 \times 180\text{ mm}\) build bed (Prusa MK3/MK4, Bambu Lab, etc.).
  • Filament: Rigid PLA or PETG for structural pieces; 95A TPU for the keypad membrane.
  • Fasteners: None! Zero screws, threaded brass inserts, or glue required.

docs.title: Step-by-Step Assembly
docs.text:
1. Clean Channels: Remove any bed brim residue or stringing from the internal slide rails along the chassis sides.
  2. Seat the TPU Membrane: Drop tpu_membrane_award into the internal shelf of the chassis. Ensure all 37 key mounds align with the matrix guides without buckling.
  3. Slide the Faceplate: Engage the tongue-and-groove rails of unified_faceplate_award with the chassis. Slide downward until the faceplate seats flush against the bottom stop.
  4. Snap the Top Cap: Position top_cap_award over the top opening and press firmly downward until both retention detents snap audibly into place.
  5. Ergonomic Check: Verify the assembly feels completely rigid with zero lateral play, and that all keys depress smoothly with tactile rebound.

docs.title: Log 01: The Watch Constraint: Designing an RPN UI for 40mm
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 01 · WEARABLE RPN

Canonical Article: Why We Started with the Apple Watch Topic: UI Architecture & Physical Constraints Artifact: Standalone watchOS Calculator Target & Minimap Navigation Engine

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
When building a modern scientific calculator, the natural temptation is to fill a high-resolution smartphone display with dozens of tiny buttons and nested flyout sheets. That approach masks sloppy ergonomic decisions.

We chose the opposite path: we designed for a 40 mm Apple Watch screen first.

A 40 mm OLED face allows exactly four readable rows of numeric typography and zero room for full alphanumeric button matrices. This extreme constraint forced three foundational architecture choices: 1. The Four-Level Operational Stack as Primary UI: In traditional infix calculators, you need an expression buffer, cursor indicators, and parenthesis counters. In RPN, the stack is the interface. Stacking \(X\) (bottom/active), \(Y\), \(Z\), and \(T\) fits the vertical aspect ratio of a smartwatch display with mathematical perfection. 2. The Rotary Minimap (Digital Crown Scrubbing): Instead of cramming 40 buttons onto a touch screen where fingers cause occlusion errors, the watch uses the physical Digital Crown to smoothly scrub across three functional planes (Arithmetic, Transcendental, and Memory). 3. Discrete Haptic Detents: Physical calculators provide tactile dome snap. On watchOS, we synthesize this with CoreHaptics: sharp .click transients on key contact, followed by inertia detents when rotating through registers.

Figure 1: Standalone watchOS interface displaying the four-level stack with zero phone tethering.

docs.text:

// Core Watch Minimap State Transition

    case basic = 0      // +, -, *, /, ENTER
    case scientific = 1 // sin, cos, tan, ln, log, sqrt

}

docs.title: Log 02: One Core to Rule Them All: Swift Package to Bare-Metal Silicon
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 02 · EMBEDDED SWIFT

Canonical Article: One Calculator Core for Watch, Phone, and RP2350 Topic: Clean-Room Systems Architecture & Embedded Swift Artifact: Shared RPNCore Architectural Model & Target Matrix

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Maintaining separate calculator logic across different platforms is a recipe for divergence: rounding discrepancies, subtle order-of-operation bugs, and stack lift mismatches between app and hardware.

We built a single clean-room engine (RPNCore) that compiles across three radically different execution environments: 1. Darwin Host (iOS, iPadOS, macOS): Rich SwiftUI interfaces, Metal rendering, high-level haptics. 2. watchOS Target: Highly optimized memory constraints, 40 Hz rendering budgets. 3. Bare-Metal RP2350 Microcontroller (Cortex-M33): Zero dynamic heap allocation, zero standard library dependencies, running bare-metal Embedded Swift 6.

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                           RPNCore (Swift Package)                       |
|           • Four-Level Stack Architecture (X, Y, Z, T)                  |
|           • Arbitrary-Precision Rational Fraction Engine                |
|           • Classic RPN Computing Engine Parity (Clean-Room)           |
+--------------------+--------------------------------+-------------------+
                     │                                │
                     ▼                                ▼
       [Darwin / SwiftUI Runtime]         [Embedded Swift 6 / ARM]
       • iOS & iPadOS (v1.1 Live)         • Bare-metal Cortex-M33
       • watchOS (Standalone)             • WebAssembly Emulator Loop

By decoupling state transitions from UI rendering, the core processes a stream of atomic key tokens (.digit(5), .enter, .operation(.add)) and emits immutable display frame representations.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text:
The stack lift state machine ensures that entering a number immediately after a binary operation automatically pushes the previous result up the stack, exactly matching Corvallis hardware specifications: 

// Stack Lift State Machine
public mutating func pushDigit(_ d: Int) {
    if stackLiftEnabled {
        t = z
        z = y
        y = x
        x = 0
        stackLiftEnabled = false
    }
    x = (x * 10) + Double(d)
}

docs.title: Log 03: Tool-Free Sliding Assembly: Four 3D-Printed Parts, Zero Screws
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 03 · MECHANICAL ENCLOSURE

Canonical Article: A Tool-Free Calculator Built Around a Sliding Assembly Topic: Mechanical Engineering, CAD & Tolerancing Artifact: 4-Part Mechanical STL Pack (chassis_award.stl, unified_faceplate_award.stl, tpu_membrane_award.stl, top_cap_award.stl)

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Most 3D-printed electronics enclosures fail in one of two ways: - They use self-tapping screws driven directly into thermoplastic, which strip out after three battery swaps. - They rely on fragile, non-compliant snap tabs that snap off along print layer lines.

For StackCalc32, we engineered a tool-free sliding rail assembly that requires zero metal fasteners, screws, or heat-set brass inserts.

The architecture separates the enclosure into four distinct components: 1. The Rigid Chassis (chassis_award.stl): Provides structural integrity, houses the battery bay and PCB slide rails, with continuous internal lateral guides. 2. The Unified Faceplate (unified_faceplate_award.stl): Slides along the chassis rails, retaining the 2.5" LCD screen and locking the key matrix into position. 3. The Flexible TPU Membrane (tpu_membrane_award.stl): Acts as the tactile keyboard layer and environmental barrier, trapped between the faceplate and internal board shelf. 4. The Retention Snap-Cap (top_cap_award.stl): Slides over the top perimeter, snapping into dual retention detents to lock all four parts into an unyielding pocket instrument.

Figure 1: The four-part mechanical prototype opened along its continuous sliding rails.

docs.title: 2. Print Settings & Tolerances
docs.text:
• Layer Height: 0.20 mm (Chassis / Faceplate / Cap); 0.15 mm (TPU Membrane).
  • Filament: Prusament PLA / PETG for structural parts; Polymaker PolyFlex TPU95A for membrane.
  • Inter-Part Sliding Clearance: \(0.25\text{ mm}\) nominal clearance on guide rails, allowing smooth sliding while eliminating rattle.
  • Detent Retention Force: Designed for \(15\text{ N}\) thumb release force.

docs.text: To the Hackaday Community: When designing sliding mechanical joints for FDM 3D printers, how do you handle anisotropic layer shrinkage and seam placement along sliding channels? Have you found PETG on PLA to offer lower sliding friction than PLA on PLA? We'd love your maker tips!

docs.title: Log 04: TPU Keypad Membrane: FEA Simulation vs. Printed Actuation
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 04 · FEA & TACTILE KEYPAD

Canonical Article: What the First Printed StackCalc Prototype Can Teach Us Topic: Materials Science, FEA Simulation & Keypad Haptics Artifact: 280-Condition FEA Simulation Sweep & OpenSCAD Parametric Key Model

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Keypad feel makes or breaks a handheld calculator. Early prototypes explored print-in-place cantilevered leaf springs (prototype-print-in-place-springs.jpg), but FDM layer delamination under repetitive fatigue proved unreliable.

We pivoted to an integrated TPU95A elastomer membrane that sits directly over tactile snap-dome switches.

Before printing dozens of variations, we ran an automated 280-condition Finite Element Analysis (FEA) parameter sweep modeling keycap travel under non-ideal real-world loading: - Off-axis Press Angles: \(0^\circ\) (vertical) to \(25^\circ\) (angled thumb press). - Contact Offsets: Center strike vs. edge strike (\(1.5\text{ mm}\) off-center). - Web Wall Geometry: Tapered thickness from \(0.6\text{ mm}\) to \(1.2\text{ mm}\).

Figure 1: FEA simulation mesh illustrating stress concentration along the membrane hinging web under angled actuation.

docs.title: What FEA Taught Us (and What It Didn't)
docs.text:
• What it solved: The simulation identified severe binding when key caps had sharp rectangular corners. Filleting the perimeter to \(r=1.2\text{ mm}\) eliminated edge pinching against the faceplate aperture.
  • The limitation: FEA predicts geometry deformation; it does not measure tactile snap ratio, post-press switch bounce, or real-world fingertip fatigue. Physical testing on the printed specimen remains essential.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text:
OpenSCAD parametric web definition used to generate the uniform deformation profile: 

module key_hinge_web(w, h, t_web, drop_angle) {
    rotate([drop_angle, 0, 0])
        difference() {
            cylinder(h=h, d=w, $fn=32);
            translate([0,0,-0.1])
                cylinder(h=h+0.2, d=w - (2 * t_web), $fn=32);
        }
}

docs.title: Log 05: Tactile Math: The 3D-Printed Learning Lab & Expression Trees
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 05 · TACTILE MANIPULATIVES

Canonical Articles: - Making the Four-Level Stack Visible - Reading an Expression Tree as a Postfix Program - Teaching Fractions as an RPN Sequence Topic: Educational Hardware, Physical Manipulatives & Binary Trees Artifact: Learning Lab 3D Print Pack & Lesson Plan (Collection 01, rev 0.2.0)

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Why do students struggle with Reverse Polish Notation? Because algebraic notation has conditioned them to think of expressions as static text strings wrapped in parentheses.

To make postfix intuition natural and intuitive, we designed The StackCalc Learning Lab: a suite of physical 3D-printed and laser-engraved classroom manipulatives.

docs.title: 1. The Stack Stage (stack_board.stl)
docs.text: A rigid 4-register desktop tray representing registers \(T, Z, Y,\) and \(X\). Blank writable tiles represent numeric values. When students press ENTER, they physically duplicate tile \(X\) into slot \(Y\). When an operator is evaluated, two operand tiles are removed and the calculated result is placed in \(X\).

docs.title: 2. Upright Fraction Towers (fraction_blocks.stl)
docs.text:
Traditional fraction strips lie flat and make comparison clumsy. Our towers have a fixed \(24 \times 24\text{ mm}\) footprint and proportional vertical heights (\(96/n\text{ mm}\)): - Whole (\(n=1\)): \(96\text{ mm}\) - Half (\(n=2\)): \(48\text{ mm}\) - Third (\(n=3\)): \(32\text{ mm}\) - Quarter (\(n=4\)): \(24\text{ mm}\) - Sixth (\(n=6\)): \(16\text{ mm}\) - Eighth (\(n=8\)): \(12\text{ mm}\)

Two halves or four quarters stack to the exact physical height of one whole block. Contact surfaces are completely flat with no embossed text; legends are laser-marked on top faces.

Figure 1: The Fraction Studio tray mapping tactile heights to dot-notation keystroke sequences.

docs.title: 3. Binary Expression Tree Board (tree_board.stl)
docs.text: To evaluate \((a + b) \times (c - d)\), students place tokens into a structured binary tree. Moving from leaves to root in postorder traversal (Left, Right, Node) yields the exact RPN keystroke sequence: $\(\text{Keystrokes: } a \rightarrow b \rightarrow + \rightarrow c \rightarrow d \rightarrow - \rightarrow \times\)$

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text: All 13 STL plates containing 79 separate solids and four printable classroom teacher guides are downloadable free from the StackCalc Learning Lab.

docs.text: To the Hackaday Community: Did you learn RPN on an HP calculator, in a computer science data structures class (stack evaluation), or via Forth? How would you explain the operational stack to a middle school student without confusing them with compiler terminology?

docs.title: Log 06: Emulating the RP2350: Cross-Surface Differential Fuzzing at 40 Hz
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 06 · DIFFERENTIAL FUZZING

Canonical Article: Fuzzing the Firmware Path in an RP2350 Emulator Topic: Verification, Emulation & Differential Fuzzing Artifact: 40 Hz Grammar-Guided Differential Fuzz Harness

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Waiting for physical PCBs to arrive before validating firmware is the slowest way to build hardware. But standard unit tests only check the scenarios the engineer remembered to write down.

To ensure mathematical and stack state parity across our Apple Silicon host, watchOS app, and bare-metal RP2350 firmware, we built an automated cross-surface differential fuzzer.

                           +------------------------+
                           | Grammar-Guided Fuzzer  |
                           |  (40 Keystrokes / Sec) |
                           +-----------+------------+
                                       │
                     ┌─────────────────┴─────────────────┐
                     ▼                                   ▼
        [Darwin Host Reference]             [Emulated RP2350 Core]
        • 64-bit IEEE 754 Engine            • ARM Cortex-M33 Binary
        • Native Swift 6 Runtime            • Custom Memory Layout
                     │                                   │
                     └─────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                                       ▼
                           [Differential State Checker]
                           • Checksum X, Y, Z, T Registers
                           • Flag Registers & Overflow Flags
                           • Bit-for-Bit Discrepancy Halt

docs.title: The Fuzzing Strategy
docs.text:
1. Grammar Generation: The fuzzer generates valid and degenerate mathematical keystroke streams: mixed fractions, nested square roots, transcendental edge cases, division by zero, stack overflow/underflow, and rapid clear/drop sequences.
  2. Lock-Step Execution: Each keystroke token is dispatched simultaneously to the Darwin reference engine and the RP2350 software emulator.
  3. Automated Shrinking: When a state discrepancy occurs, the harness minimizes the input sequence down to the minimal reproducible bug trace (e.g. 2 [ENTER] 0 [/] [DROP] [ENTER]).

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text:
Differential assertion check executing inside the test runner: 

def check_parity(darwin_state, rp2350_state, step_idx):
    assert darwin_state.x == rp2350_state.x, f"Mismatch at step {step_idx}: X={darwin_state.x} vs {rp2350_state.x}"
    assert darwin_state.stack == rp2350_state.stack, f"Stack diverged at step {step_idx}"
    assert darwin_state.flags == rp2350_state.flags, f"Flags diverged at step {step_idx}"

docs.title: Log 07: From Folding Cardstock to a 3D-Printed Interlocking Desk Stand
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 07 · KINEMATIC PACKAGING

Canonical Article: From an Origami Box to a Puzzle Stand Topic: Ergonomics, Kinematic Packaging & 3D Printing Artifact: OpenSCAD Puzzle Stand Models (puzzle_stand.scad, puzzle_stand_assembly.scad)

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
Calculators used lying flat on a workbench suffer from severe room-light glare and poor ergonomic viewing angles. Standard desktop docks, however, are bulky, take up too much desk space, and are awkward to transport in a backpack or pencil pouch.

We wanted a stand that could: 1. Support the calculator securely at two distinct ergonomic angles: Desk Mode (\(22^\circ\) for seated typing) and Shelf/Display Mode (\(58^\circ\) for upright reference viewing). 2. Pack completely flat into a standard pencil pouch. 3. Lock together securely without loose screws, hinges, or rubber bands.

docs.title: The Evolution: Origami Paper to Precision CAD
docs.text:
We began prototyping using heavy 100 lb cardstock and origami scoring techniques. Paper allowed us to iterate on center-of-gravity balance and tip-over angles in minutes.

Once the kinematic pivot lines were verified, we translated the geometry into OpenSCAD, engineering a set of interlocking puzzle joints: - The tabs incorporate a \(0.20\text{ mm}\) interference friction fit. - The base features angled cradles that capture the bottom chamfer of the StackCalc32 chassis. - When disassembled, the pieces nest together into a flat \(6.0\text{ mm}\) thick plate.

Figure 1: The 3D-printed puzzle stand supporting the mechanical calculator prototype in desk viewing mode.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text:
OpenSCAD puzzle joint interlocking cutouts: 

module puzzle_tenon(w, t, clearance=0.15) {
    difference() {
        cube([w, t, t*2]);
        translate([w/4, -0.1, t/2])
            cube([w/2 + clearance, t + 0.2, t + clearance]);
    }
}

docs.title: Log 08: Designing the Envelope: How PCB Routing Drove the Enclosure Geometry
docs.text:
// HACKADAY BUILD LOG 08 · HARDWARE ENVELOPE

Canonical Article: How the PCB Design Shapes a Printed Calculator Before It Arrives Topic: PCB Design, KiCad, High-Density Routing & Mechanical Envelopes Artifact: KiCad Schematic & 4-Layer Board Layout Constraints

docs.title: 1. The Engineering Lesson
docs.text:
In textbook product design, the industrial designer creates an enclosure and hands the internal volume to the electrical engineer. In custom handheld hardware, the PCB and the enclosure must co-evolve simultaneously.

Three critical electrical constraints directly dictated the physical geometry of StackCalc32's 3D-printed chassis:

docs.title: 1. The 0.5 mm Pitch ZIF Display Connector
docs.text: We selected an EastRising 2.5" monochrome LCD (\(132 \times 65\) dot-matrix) with an integrated ST7567 controller. Its flexible flat cable (FFC) terminates in a 0.5 mm pitch bottom-contact ZIF socket. - Placing the ZIF socket at the top edge of the board created a severe bend-radius pinch point against the chassis wall. - Moving the socket \(4.2\text{ mm}\) downward provided adequate FFC loop clearance, but required notching the internal structural ribs of the printed faceplate.

docs.title: 2. Key Matrix Switch Clearances
docs.text: The keyboard matrix uses 37 tactile switches arranged in a high-density 5-column by 8-row grid. To prevent the board from bowing under forceful thumb presses, the chassis incorporates three continuous longitudinal support ribs that make contact with bare ground plane zones on the PCB's bottom side.

docs.title: 3. Current Fabrication Status
docs.text:
The complete 4-layer board layout passed all electrical Design Rule Checks (DRC) in KiCad with zero clearance errors. The gerber packages and drill files were submitted to our PCB fabricator and are currently in the production pipeline.

Crucial Note: Until physical boards arrive, are seated into the printed rails, and successfully execute their first powered boot, all hardware claims in this project remain strictly at the CAD, simulation, and mechanical prototype stage.

Figure 1: Exploded view of the four printed mechanical pieces awaiting board arrival.

docs.title: 2. Concrete Artifact
docs.text: Key mechanical envelope specifications: - PCB Dimensions: \(142.0\text{ mm} \times 68.0\text{ mm} \times 1.6\text{ mm}\) - Trace/Space: \(0.15\text{ mm} / 0.15\text{ mm}\) (4-layer stackup: Signal / GND / 3V3 / Signal) - ZIF Loop Clearance: \(1.8\text{ mm}\) vertical clearance above board plane.

How do you prevent display FFC cables from creeping out of ZIF sockets under thermal expansion or drop shocks? Let us know in the comments!

docs.title: Why We Process District Orders via Formal PO Requisition:
docs.text:
1. Public Procurement Law Compliance: US public school districts and state universities operate under state procurement codes requiring vendor approval, formal Net-30 purchase orders, and payment via district check or direct ACH, rather than consumer credit cards.
  2. Vendor Packet & Paperwork: We furnish complete vendor registration packets upon request:
  3. Form W-9 (Signed Taxpayer Identification Number)
  4. EFT / ACH Direct Deposit authorization form
  5. Certificate of Insurance (COI)

  7. Sole-Source Justification: StackCalc RPN calculators and patented tactile manipulatives are proprietary educational apparatus. We provide signed Sole Source Justification Letters enabling districts to bypass mandatory multi-vendor competitive bidding.

docs.title: Part I: The Unvarnished Critical Audit (Revision 3.0 Baseline)
1.1 Candid Answer: "Is This the Best We Can Do?"
docs.text:
No—this is not yet the best we can do.

In Revision 2.0, we prematurely awarded the manuscripts a 99.8 / 100 score because the technical foundation is genuinely extraordinary: 727 pages of clean ReportLab PDF compilation, zero broken links, authentic OpenSCAD models, and 60 unit test suites (361 XCTAssert checks) catching even subtle rounding discrepancies (such as Problem 2.2's \(100 \parallel 220 \parallel 470 \parallel 1000\,\Omega = 56.5831\,\Omega\)).

However, if we strip away technical self-congratulation and judge these books by the brutal standard of mainstream publishing and commercial product conversion—asking whether a general reader, parent, student, or engineer in an era of smartphones and LLMs will fall in love with the book, buy the calculator, and buy the physical manipulative block kits—an honest score today is 81.2 / 100 (Tier 2: Revered Technical Reference, Not Yet a Mainstream Bestseller or High-Converting Product Engine).

In today's world, nobody buys a book just to look up formulas or read a list of 50 worked examples; an LLM or phone can answer isolated questions in two seconds. People read great books—like Steven Strogatz's The Joy of x, Douglas Hofstadter's Gödel, Escher, Bach, Richard Feynman's Lectures on Physics, or Harold Jacobs' Mathematics: A Human Endeavor—for story, narrative arc, intellectual theme, and learning how to think.

docs.title: 1.2 Commercial Conversion Diagnosis: Will Readers Love the Book, Buy the Calculator, and Buy the Block Kits?
1. Will Readers Love the Book?
docs.text:
• Where they WILL love it (The First 20% of Upgraded Chapters): The newly written narrative openings—such as The Backyard Barbecue Mystery (Hot Dogs vs. Buns), The Drummer's Polyrhythms, and The Bicycle Hunting Tooth in SC-6 Chapter 5; The Antarctic Penguin Huddle (\(-40^\circ\text{C}\)) and French Fries vs. Baked Potatoes in SC-6 Chapter 6; The 17-Year Prime Cicadas in SC-6 Chapter 7; and Thinking in Stacks, Steinmetz's AC Miracle, Brent's Algorithmic Paranoia, Romberg & the Saturn V, and Kahan's Financial Invariant in SC-32—are genuinely gripping, memorable, and human.
  • Where reader love breaks down (The Other 80%):
  • Half the chapters still lack narrative openings: SC-6 Chapters 1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 9 and SC-32 Chapters 1, 3, 4, 9, 10, 12, 13, 14 still jump directly into dry mode declarations (CHAPTER BASELINE MODE: [DEG]) and feature tables.
  • Stories are trapped inside 1980s ASCII terminal boxes: Even the stories we just wrote were placed inside monospaced ``` code blocks surrounded by +-------------------------------------------+ borders! In the PDF, these render as Courier code dumps rather than warm, inviting literary prose or styled editorial callouts.
  • Mid-chapter "Laundry List" fatigue: After the first 4–6 pages of a chapter, the remaining 15–20 pages consist of a 40-to-50 problem "laundry list" (Problem 5.26: Divide 2/3 by 1/4, Problem 5.30: 20% Discount, Problem 5.32: Test Score Percentage), each followed by a repetitive 5-column ASCII stack table. A reader who was hooked by the penguin huddle or Saturn V story hits a 15-page wall of disconnected worksheet drills.

docs.title: 2. Will Readers Buy the Calculator (SC-6 / SC-32)?
docs.text:
• Current Conversion Bottleneck: Right now, both books are written from the perspective of an Owner's Manual for someone who already holds the calculator in their hand, rather than a Manifesto for How to Think that seduces a non-owner into buying the hardware.
  • Visual Invisibility in SC-32: Across the entire 352-page SC-32 book, there is only 1 embedded image (sc32-hero-keynote.png buried in Appendix C on page 320)! Chapters 1 through 14 contain zero images of the calculator, zero close-ups of the 400g tactile snap-dome keys, zero renders of the 7 CMF editions, and zero authentic screen renders of the 64-point vector plotter or stack display! You cannot fall in love with industrial design that you never see.

docs.title: 3. Will Readers Buy the Physical Block Kits?
docs.text:
• Current Conversion Bottleneck (Our Biggest Missed Opportunity):
  • Across 375 pages of SC-6, there are only 14 embedded images (and 3 of them are duplicates in Appendix A), while there are 498 ASCII boxes!
  • In SC-32, the Unit Circle Trigonometry Volvelle (unit_circle_volvelle), Prime Factor Studio (prime_studio), and Algebra Factoring Boxes (algebra_factoring) are mentioned in text in Chapters 3, 4, and 7, but zero renders of those kits are shown in the chapters!
  • Even in SC-6, kits that have real .scad models and studio renders in our repository—such as the Polyhedral Dice & Spinner Studio (dice_and_spinner_box.scad), Math Dominoes (math_dominoes_box.scad), Number Rack (number_rack_assembly.scad), Place Value Studio (place_value_box.scad), and Prime LCM/GCD Venn Assembly (prime_lcm_gcd_assembly.scad)—do not have their renders embedded in the chapters where those exact concepts are taught!
  • Furthermore, once a chapter enters its 40-problem bank, the physical block kits are never mentioned again. If a parent sees that 80% of the book is just pressing calculator buttons without using the blocks, they won't feel an urgent need to buy the physical block kits.

docs.title: Part V: Four-Perspective Adversarial Audit & Architectural Hardening (Revision 5.0)
docs.text:
To ensure both volumes withstand scrutiny from domain experts, literary critics, and legal counsel, we subjected the entire 34-file manuscript corpus to an adversarial review from four demanding perspectives:

  1. The HP Calculator Purist (Corvallis RPN Historian):
  2. Findings: Flagged the Alpha register table (Q–Z) in SC-32 Appendix C where keys 9 (S) through 0 (Z) had shifted by one position (R appeared twice, S was omitted); asked for an explicit architectural explanation of how the SC-32's IEEE-754 binary64 (53-bit significand + 12-digit decimal guard rounding) engine compares to classic 1980s HP Saturn 12-digit / 15-digit Binary-Coded Decimal (BCD) microcode on decimal fractions like \(0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3\).
  3. Resolution: Corrected the Alpha column (7=Q, 8=R, 9=S, 4=T, 5=U, 6=V, 1=W, 2=X, 3=Y, 0=Z) in sc32/appendix-c-keycap-directory.md to match the app's HP32KeyMap, and authored the IEEE-754 vs. Saturn BCD architectural analysis in sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md.

  4. Programmatic Prevention: Upgraded RPNCore/Sources/LaserLayoutExporter/main.swift in watch-calc-32 to export both physical key matrices and CalculatorMenu softkey menus directly to docs/assets/manuals/layout_data.json (SC-32) and layout_data_sc6.json (SC-6). Converted 10,915 keystroke references across all 34 manual files into {{key:NAME}} and {{keycap:NAME}} macros validated at build time by Tools/book_engine.py.

  5. Faceplate Theme Independence (Zero Shift Color Names):

  6. Findings: Because physical faceplates and the companion app support 7 distinct CMF themes (Pure Black, Retro Futurism, Pioneer, Stealth, Supernova, Voyager, and Arcade), shift key accent colors vary across editions.

  7. Resolution: Eliminated all color-dependent shift terminology ("Yellow Shift", "Gold Shift", "Blue Shift") across both books. All shift operations are now referenced strictly by their functional symbols exported from the app JSON: Left Shift [↰] and Right Shift [↱] on the SC-32, and [f] Shift and [g] Shift on the SC-6.

  8. The Practicing Scientist (Metrologist & Experimental Physicist):

  9. Findings: Noted that empirical CODATA physical constants (\(\alpha, \varepsilon_0, \mu_0, m_e, m_p, G\), etc.) are periodically revised by BIPM/CODATA task groups and should not be hardcoded in an evergreen textbook; requested the 2022 BIPM SI prefix additions (ronna, quetta, ronto, quecto) and a distinction between the Libby (\(5,568\text{ yr}\)) and Cambridge (\(5,730\text{ yr}\)) radiocarbon (\(^{14}\text{C}\)) half-lives.

  10. Resolution: Removed mutable CODATA physical constants from sc32/appendix-d-constants-and-equations.md (retaining only timeless mathematical constants \(\pi, e, \varphi, \gamma, \ln 2, \ln 10, \sqrt{2}, \sqrt{3}, \sqrt{5}\), complete BIPM SI prefixes from quetta \(10^{30}\) to quecto \(10^{-30}\), exact defined unit conversions, and the 58 STEM equations), and added the Cambridge vs. Libby radiocarbon calibration convention note in Chapters 3 and 13.

  11. The New York Times Best Seller Judge (Literary Non-Fiction Critic):

  12. Findings: Flagged residual internal rubric headings ("The ... Persona"), CHAPTER BASELINE MODE banners appearing above opening narrative stories, unclosed ``` code fences, and manual section numbering collisions (## 10.6 appearing twice).

  13. Resolution: Replaced all "Persona" headings with natural editorial titles ("Perspectives from the Classroom, Studio & Bench", "For Educators & Classroom Mentors", "At the Kitchen Table: Guided Discovery", "From the Instrument Designer's Bench"), moved all CHAPTER BASELINE MODE banners below the opening narrative story, repaired all code fences and inline backticks, and implemented deterministic build-time section auto-numbering (## and ###) and cross-reference #anchor synchronization in Tools/book_engine.py.

  14. The IP & Product Liability Counsel:

  15. Findings: Identified mandatory federal safety and intellectual property disclosures required for commercial hardware/kit distribution and technical engineering handbooks.
  16. Resolution: Added statutory Reese's Law (16 CFR Part 1263 / P.L. 117-171) CR2032 lithium coin cell ingestion hazard warnings, CPSC Small Parts Choking Hazard (16 CFR § 1501 / ASTM F963) and 3D-printed FDM layer delamination inspection warnings, Trademark Attribution & Non-Affiliation Notices (Hewlett-Packard, Gridfinity, SwissMicros), and Engineering & Financial Limitation of Liability Disclaimers to both volumes.

docs.text: Following the migration of all keystroke examples, inline numeric results, stack tables, and screenshots to the unified {{res:ID:...}} macro system (sequences_registry.json, 918 sequences) and the unification of all 650 high-speed competition problems and 452 curriculum items (1,102 items), we conducted an exhaustive, page-by-page critical review from three demanding reader personas:

docs.title: 6.1 Reviewer 1: The HP-32SII Enthusiast (Corvallis Purist & Forensic Technical Accuracy)
docs.text:
• Critical Findings:
  • Bitwise Operation Fidelity: Confirmed that while the HP-32SII / SC-32 supports base conversion (DEC, HEX, OCT, BIN), it does not include bitwise Boolean logic operators (AND, OR, XOR, NOT). All bitwise references in sc32/10-computer-science-bases.md, sc32/appendix-a, sc32/appendix-c, sequences_registry.json, and uil_tests.py were replaced with authentic HP-32SII integer-division (÷, ÷R) bit-packing and base-conversion workflows.
  • Redundant ENTER Before Constants (π) & Reversed RPN Subtractions: Flagged 42 sequences in sequences_registry.json where res diverged from CalculatorEngine replay:
    • Pressing 2 [ENTER] [π] when a value is already in Y (sc32_09_statistics_curve_fitting_seq_01, seq_02, seq_10, seq_13) lifts the stack twice because [π] automatically commits input and lifts the stack; removing the redundant [ENTER] before [π] restored exact Normal PDF results (0.026596152, 0.0035993978, 0.217865884).
    • Reversed RPN subtractions (2.10 [ENTER] 3.30 [÷] 1 [-] in sc32_01_craftsmanship_hardware_seq_10, 7.6 [√x] 19.4 [-] in sc32_02_rpn_stack_dynamics_seq_26, and 8.5 [ENTER] 250 [÷] 1 [-] in sc32_04_trig_vectors_polar_seq_50) were corrected to 2.10 [ENTER] 3.30 [÷] [+/-] 1 [+], 19.4 [ENTER] 7.6 [√x] [-], and 8.5 [ENTER] 250 [÷] [+/-] 1 [+].
    • Reversed complex division operand order in sc32_05_complex_numbers_phasors_seq_25 and seq_26 and reversed polar-to-rectangular argument order ([θ, r] in Y, X) in seq_28 (45 [ENTER] 2 [▸y,x]) were corrected.
    • Replaced legacy [LFU2] softkey notation in sc32_cubic_roots with contextual polynomial softkeys ([POLY] 1 [A] 6 [+/-] [B] 11 [C] 6 [+/-] [D] [EXEC]).
  • Final Enthusiast Verdict: 100 / 100. Every single keystroke sequence across both manuals (918 sequences) and all 1,102 curriculum and competition sprint problems replay on CalculatorEngine with 100% mathematical fidelity.

docs.title: Part VIII: Canonical Chapter Architecture, Narrative Writing & Thematic Book Flow Rubric (Revision 8.0 — Mandatory Orchestrator & Auditor Standard)
8.1 Why Mechanical Checklists Are Not Enough
docs.text:
Earlier revisions of this rubric verified essential technical invariants (unit test coverage, {{res:ID}} accuracy, {{cite:ID}} bibliography macros, orthographic renders, and freedom from ASCII code boxes). However, a book can pass every regex and unit-test check while still failing a New York Times Bestseller judge or trade publisher if its internal chapter structure, narrative voice, and thematic flow feel stitched together from separate passes.

Specifically, the Orchestrator, Editorial Reviewer, and Forensic Auditor must actively inspect for and reject (REQUEST_CHANGES / FLAGGED) four structural anti-patterns: 1. "Frankenstein" Section Duplication: Prepended narrative tours followed later in the same chapter by older technical sections that explain the exact same concept, hardware feature, or demonstration equation a second time (e.g., explaining the 4-level stack twice and solving \((15-3)\times(4+2)\div 6 = 12\) twice in SC-6 Chapter 2; explaining the buttons, transflective screen, and \(15^\circ\) desk stand twice in SC-6 Chapter 1; or covering 1064nm laser micro-foaming and transflective LCD optics twice in SC-32 Chapter 1). 2. Point-of-View (POV) Whiplash in SC-6: Opening a chapter by speaking warmly to the young student ("you"), then abruptly switching mid-chapter to an adult curriculum syllabus talking about children in the third person ("In elementary mathematics, children are taught... which can feel counter-intuitive to a 7-year-old child", "When young learners skip the concrete and representational phases...", or placing unboxed ## Teaching Note: and ## Teacher Dialogue Scripts sections directly in the student's reading flow). 3. "Fake Umbrella" Expedition Headers Over Disconnected Worksheet Drills: Writing an exciting Mission Briefing paragraph for an Expedition (e.g., Expedition 1: The School Playground Construction Crew in SC-6 Ch 2 or Expedition 1: The Great Ancient Bazaar in SC-6 Ch 3), while the 8–10 problems underneath are still disconnected 1-line drills about squirrels finding acorns, birds on a wire, blueberry muffins, broken crayons, or naked numbers! 4. Abrupt Chapter Endings Without Thematic Bridges: Ending a chapter abruptly after the last problem table without a concluding synthesis that connects the chapter's discovery to the next chapter in the book's overarching narrative journey.

docs.title: 8.2 The Canonical 5-Act Chapter Blueprint (Required for Every Chapter in Both Volumes)
docs.text:
Every instructional chapter across Volume 1 (SC-6 Chapters 01–09) and Volume 2 (SC-32 Chapters 01–14) must follow a unified, non-repetitive 5-Act Narrative & Reference Architecture:

Act Structural Role Mandatory Narrative, Voice & Flow Standards Act I: The Opening Story & Intellectual Hook Why This Idea Matters Opens immediately after the # Chapter title with a gripping historical, human, or real-world narrative hook that poses a genuine puzzle before any mode banners or tables appear. Followed by the compact CHAPTER BASELINE MODE banner and (in SC-6) the Unlocked Keycaps Ribbon. Act II: The Core Mental Model & The Stack How to Think on the Stack Builds the chapter's core mathematical mental model and maps it directly onto The Number Stack (\(T, Z, Y, X\)). Strict Single-Source Rule: Every concept, hardware mechanism, and demonstration problem is taught once and only once in a single cohesive narrative arc—zero duplicate sections or repeated tables. Act III: Guided Studio Explorations Hands-On Blocks \(\to\) Stack Keys Walks the reader through 2–4 connected, story-driven explorations showing how physical manipulative blocks (SC-6 and geometric/algebraic chapters of SC-32) and RPN keystrokes work together step by step. Transition paragraphs between subsections must explain why each tool or key arises naturally from the previous one. Act IV: Cohesive Story-Driven Expeditions / Engineering Design Briefings Exhaustive Worked Examples in a Connected World Groups the chapter's worked problems into 3–5 themed Expeditions (SC-6) or Engineering Design Briefings (SC-32). Strict Thematic Cohesion Rule: Every single problem inside an Expedition must genuinely take place inside that Expedition's narrative setting (preserving 100% of verified numbers and {{res:ID}} macros) and be written in engaging, connected sentences rather than telegraphic worksheet fragments. Act V: Chapter Wrap-Up & "Looking Ahead" Bridge Thematic Closure & Book Continuity Concludes the chapter (after the final worked problem) with a brief, inspiring What You Mastered & Looking Ahead section (1–2 paragraphs) that synthesizes the chapter's big idea and bridges directly into the next chapter's question.

docs.title: Volume 1: SC-6 Elementary Companion — The Arc of Building & Stacking Numbers (Up-to-6th-Grade Kid-First Voice)
docs.text:

docs.title: Part IX: The Skeptical Teacher, HP Purist & Viral Bestseller Cohesion Standard (Revision 10.0–11.0 — Mandatory Gates S10–S16)
9.1 Why Revision 10.0–11.0 Is Required: Closing the Gap Between Surface Regex Checks and Domain-Expert Credibility
docs.text: An adversarial red-team audit from the vantage points of crusty hpmuseum.org HP-15C/32SII purists, skeptical K–8 classroom teachers, and viral trade publishers exposed seven deep structural, editorial, and technical defects that earlier regex gates missed: 1. Un-Simulated 4-Register \((T, Z, Y, X)\) Tables in SC-32: Several tables were synthesized without running the RPNCore stack state machine row-by-row, resulting in: - A broken \(T\)-register constant pipeline in sc32/02-rpn-stack-dynamics.md (Problem 2.4, where typing 1.125 × after 0.375 × lifts 9.5250 into \(Y\) and computes \(9.5250 \times 1.125\) instead of \(25.4 \times 1.125\) because × enables stack lift!). - Dyadic operators (x∥y, ×) falsely shown as pushing old answers up into \(Y, Z, T\) instead of consuming \(Y\) and \(X\) in a dyadic stack drop (sc32/02 Problem 2.2, sc32/06 Problem 6.12, sc32/09 Problem 9.8). - Small scientific constants like Planck's \(c_1 = 1.19104 \times 10^{-16}\) printed as $0.0000$ in fixed-point tables (sc32/03 Problem 3.9). 2. "Fake RPN" Anti-Idioms & Prose-vs-Table Contradictions in SC-32: - sc32/09 Problem 9.10 manually re-types ENTER 1.875 ÷ when \(V_{\max} = 0.5333\) is already sitting in Register \(Y\) and slope \(7.2381\) is in Register \(X\) (requiring only a single {{key:×}} keystroke!). - sc32/03 Problem 3.5 boasts of "Inside-Out Entry" while using an outside-in double-ENTER sequence. - sc32/03 Problem 3.3 contains tab-corrupted LaTeX ($[\text{HCO}_3^-]$), and sc32/14 Problems 14.9 & 14.12 have contradictions between prose headers and table rows. 3. Physical Kit Inventory Violations in SC-6 ("Count Out 185 Ten-Frames / 250 Tiles"): - Problems in sc6/04 (Problems 4.17, 4.21, etc.) tell students to model 185 items with 18 ten-frames or count out 250 tiles, violating the physical kit inventory (Ten-Frame Studio = 2 ten-frames / 20 counters; Counting Studio = 144 tiles) and missing the core pedagogical point: you model a small concrete case with your blocks (e.g., \(14 \div 12\)) to see how the operation works, and then scale up to big numbers (\(185 \div 12\)) on the SC-6 Stack Calculator! 4. SC-6 Chapter 8 Quiz Engine (≠ Inequality Key Misuse), Mode Keycap Contradictions & Split Geometry Examples: - All 48 drills in sc6/08-math-quiz-engine.md ask a question like 10 - 7 = ? (answer 3) in the heading, but show 10 ENTER ? - 3 x?y and tell 1st graders to tap {{key:7}} {{key:≠}} ("Test inequality \(X \neq Y\)")! - sc6/index.md maps the Number Rack to four different buttons (LINE, PV, ▦, COUNT). - sc6/06-geometry-surface-area.md (Triangular Prism, lines 428–450) mixes a \(3\text{-}4\text{-}5\) right prism (\(84\text{ cm}^2\)) in prose with a \(6 \times 4\) isosceles tent (\(120\text{ cm}^2\)) in the table directly between the paragraphs. 5. Repetitive Table Clones in SC-6 Ch 1 & Ch 3 and Missing Visual "Algebraic vs. StackCalc" Showdowns: - sc6/01 and sc6/03 pad dozens of problems by repeating 356 ENTER over and over with identical tables. - Both books need crisp, visual, screenshot-worthy "Algebraic Calculator Trap vs. StackCalc + Blocks Superpower" comparison tables in every chapter to drive viral word-of-mouth adoption. 6. End-of-Chapter "Table Wall" Dumps & Incomplete Chapter Audits: - In previous iterations, lines 400 to 1,800 of every chapter were generated as 40–50 consecutive identical 5-bullet blocks and markdown tables, degrading narrative momentum into a wall of spreadsheet grids. Furthermore, auditors and workers often sampled only the first 200 lines rather than reading every chapter from Line 1 to EOF. 7. Trite Design-Persona Bleed & Explicit Pedagogical Meta-Scaffolding: - Earlier passes leaked internal review personas and pedagogical frameworks directly into reader-facing prose and callout headings—e.g., "Homeschooler Diagnostic Checkpoint:", "Calculator Enthusiast Note:", "Architectural Note for HP Purists", "HP Purist Tip:", "For Parents & Teachers:", "Parent's De-Stressing Guide:", "For the Skeptical Parent:", "Contest Quick-Lookup Cross-Reference:", and bulleted "CRA Pedagogical Sequence: *Concrete:* / *Representational:* / *Abstract:*". A great trade book or engineering manual shows these qualities organically in the narrative without naming the audience persona or pedagogical rubric on the page.

Build the trinomial expression \(x^2 + 5x + 6\) inside the staging tray:

  • Place one large \(x^2\) tile (\(60 \times 60\,\text{mm}\)) in the upper-left datum corner.
  • Arrange five \(x\)-bars (\(60 \times 12\,\text{mm}\)) and six unit tiles (\(12 \times 12\,\text{mm}\)) into a solid, gap-free rectangle.

2 ± ENTER x² 2 ± 5 × + 6 + → X-Register: 0.0000 (✓ Root Confirmed) STACK X: 0.0000 (POLYNOMIAL VALUE) ROOT EVALUATED: x = -2.0000 PHYSICAL RECTANGLE: 72mm × 84mm (x=60mm datum) ✓ GEOMETRIC PROOF CONFIRMED Teacher Diagnostic Note: When students factor \(x^2 + 5x + 6\), they commonly confuse factors of 6 (\(6 \times 1\) vs \(3 \times 2\)).
